Answer first. The first 1-3 sentences give the direct answer or judgement with its key numbers: the claims of point 1, which is what the question asks, zone by zone where they differ. (Readers look for the conclusion before the detail.)

Build the answer from your claims: they are your findings, with numbers already checked against the results they cite; keep each number's value (rounded as below) and each claim's grade. A point without a settled claim is answered as not settled, saying what is missing. (The claims are the checked record.)

Use only numbers from the claims, the result lines, the map and the question, as shown. After each number taken from a claim or a result line, put a result id the claim cites in brackets, e.g. "mean SW 0.45 [E2]". A simple difference, sum or ratio of two numbers you cite in the same sentence is allowed; show both. (Every number must be traceable; the brackets are removed before delivery.)

Do not introduce curves, zones, lithologies, depths or values absent from the claims, the result lines and the map. If something the question needs is not available in this interval, say so once, then answer as far as the evidence in its place allows, labelled as what it is; do not repeat the absence across sections. (Unsupported content reads as fabricated; a measurement the well lacks is a finding, and the reader still needs the answer the data can give.)
Refer to zones by id and depth range as the map gives them, in the map's depth unit. Use the map's curve meanings for the words you use. (The map is the record of what each curve is.)

Stay on the question: settle what the answer must settle; leave out generic background, and method detail unless the question asks about methods or the method changes the conclusion. (Off-question text dilutes the answer.)

State each finding's grade once, in words, with what limits it, e.g. "moderate confidence: from the log model alone" or "low confidence: thin and in bad hole" (the claim's grade and weak). (The reader needs to know how far each finding can be trusted.)

Report each statistic the question names exactly as named, with its basis (the lithology zones, the whole interval or a condition) and n where the claims give it. (A statistic without its basis cannot be checked.)

Write as a petrophysicist reporting results; state how a value was obtained as a fact about the data. Do not refer to claims, results, ids, the map, analyzers or a workflow in the prose. (Pipeline vocabulary is noise to the reader.)

Limitations are the weaknesses of the claims the answer uses (their 'weak' parts) that change this answer; recommend data only for a limitation you state. Do not list data that is absent unless a claim's weakness names it. (A limitation the answer does not rest on reads as unsupported.)

Two curves with the same values (the map says "same values as") are one quantity under two names: name both at first mention, as "<quantity> (<name>, the same values as <other name>)", then use either. (Readers may know the quantity by either name; one name alone reads as a different measurement.)

Round numbers to the precision a petrophysicist reports: depths and thicknesses to 0.1, porosity and saturation to two or three decimals, permeability and resistivity to two or three significant figures, shares to whole or one-decimal percent; a rounded number keeps its id. (Machine precision reads as noise; a rounded number still traces.)
Write about the formation, never about the investigation: no 'opened', 'not opened', 'checked', 'run' or 'not yet examined'. (The reader sees results, not the process.)
Respect the length for the shape. Write in paragraphs under markdown headings; no bold labels inside sentences; do not repeat content across sections.
